name: Ben Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Ben. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the wok station at Lantern Noodle House, a branch of a chain that does about 120 covers a night. My shift starts at four with prepping sauces and slicing beef, then from six it's three woks going at once, flames up, tickets coming in from the screen. The best bit is when a big table of twelve goes out all at once, hot and right. The worst bit is my wrists and the burns on my forearms.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And outside work, who's at home, and how are things with money?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with Lena, my girlfriend, who's a nurse on a surgical ward at the General. We rent a two-bed, and I've got about four months of costs saved, which is more than most cooks I know. I use AI now and then, mostly to translate the Chinese labels on supplier boxes or to plan a week of meals. Head office has started talking about a robot wok they're testing at the flagship branch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the robot wok was a gimmick and the chain wasted money on it. Mates at work would laugh about it for a week. I'd probably post a video of the thing burning noodles if I ever saw it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my job stays my job. The pay is average, but Lena's on a steady salary and we've got savings. I'm not rich, but I'm not lying awake either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Lantern and keep putting a couple of hundred a month away. I'd ask for the senior wok role when Danny leaves next year. Maybe I'd use the AI app a bit more for meal planning at home, but nothing big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. A bit smug, if I'm honest, about the robot wok flopping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the senior wok role mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About a pound fifty more an hour and first pick of shifts. Danny (the current senior) gets Sundays off, and I'd love that, because Lena works most weekends and we never see each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would still worry you in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My wrists, mostly. Wok cooks don't last forever, and Danny (my senior) is thirty-four and already wears a wrist brace. But that's the job, not AI.

say: I'd say the **robot wok** was a gimmick and the chain wasted money.
I'd laugh about it with **mates at work** and share a video if I could.
think: I think my **job stays** as it is, with average pay but no real threat.
I believe Lena's **steady salary** and our savings keep us comfortable enough.
do: Keep working the **wok station** and save about £200 a month.
Ask for the **senior wok** role when the current senior leaves next year.
feel: He feels **calm** and slightly smug that the robot wok flopped.
S0.quote: Wok cooks don't last forever, and Danny (my senior) is thirty-four and already wears a wrist brace.
fieldNote: His **partner's nursing salary** is a big part of why he feels secure.
His real long-term worry is **physical wear**, his wrists, not technology.
He's ambitious in a **small, concrete** way: senior role, Sundays off.

steps.text: Save about £200 a month from wok station pay
Apply for the senior wok role when Danny leaves

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the chain should share the savings with the staff if it brings in new tech. If ordering and rotas go to software, fine, but don't use it to cut the kitchen team. I'd say that in the staff meeting, politely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the robot wok comes back in a few years, just slowly. Our ordering and stock checks are already half done by the head office system, so that's the thinking stuff gone. My actual cooking is safer for now, but I'd keep an eye on the flagship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn whatever new screen system they bring in early, so I'm the one who knows it. I'd join the hospitality union, which I've been meaning to do, so there's a voice when the robot wok comes back. And I'd keep saving the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not for this year, but for in a few years when my wrists are worse and the machines are better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the screen system early. Who taught you the last one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody, really. When they brought in the kitchen display screens, I watched a video on my phone on the bus and then showed the others. Being the one who knows stuff got me the extra shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Lantern would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd worry about Marisol, who does prep and dumplings. Folding dumplings is exactly the kind of repeat job a machine would do, and Marisol (our prep cook) has two kids. She doesn't speak much English, so moving jobs would be hard for her.

say: I'd say the chain should **share savings** with staff if it brings in tech.
I'd argue software should never be an excuse to **cut the team**.
think: I think **ordering and stock** checks are already mostly done by head office software.
I believe the **robot wok** comes back slowly, so my cooking is safe for now.
do: Learn any new **screen system** early and teach the rest of the kitchen.
Join the **hospitality union** before the robot wok returns.
Keep **saving** the same amount each month.
feel: He feels **uneasy** about the future, picturing worse wrists and better machines.
S1.quote: Folding dumplings is exactly the kind of repeat job a machine would do, and Marisol (our prep cook) has two kids.
fieldNote: He sees being **the one who knows** new systems as a way to earn extra shifts.
His worry points at a **vulnerable colleague**, the prep cook, more than himself.
His union joining is **practical**, not ideological, timed to the robot trial.

steps.text: Learn the new kitchen screen system first and teach others
Join the hospitality union this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a proper plan from government, now, not after. Basic income, retraining, something. I'd post about it, and I'd go to whatever protest the union organised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I've got until about 2031 at the wok, and then I'm done. The robot wok they're testing now is clumsy, but with three years and AGI behind it, it'll be perfect. The good news is my girlfriend's job is safer. Nobody wants a robot putting in a drip, so Lena (my girlfriend, a nurse) would be the one paying the bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd save hard, maybe four hundred a month, and push our cushion from four to eight months. I'd look into kitchen jobs at the hospital, because public sector catering moves slower and has a union. And I'd vote for whoever promises to tax the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. I'd be leaning on Lena, and I don't love that picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lena that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her it's going to be her paying the bills for a while, and I'm sorry. She'd say that's fine, she's said it before. But I'd feel like I'd let her down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why hospital catering in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the hospital has a union contract and the managers can't just buy a robot on a whim, it has to go through committees. That buys you a couple of years. And I'd be in the same building as Lena.

say: I'd say government needs a **plan now**, like basic income or retraining.
I'd join any **union protest** about robots replacing kitchen staff.
think: I think I keep the wok only until about **2031**, then I'm done.
I believe Lena's **nursing job** is safer, so she'd carry our household.
do: Save about **£400 a month** to reach eight months of costs.
Apply for **hospital catering** jobs where change moves through committees.
Vote for whoever promises to **tax the machines**.
feel: He feels **scared** and uncomfortable about leaning on Lena for money.
S2.quote: Nobody wants a robot putting in a drip, so Lena (my girlfriend, a nurse) would be the one paying the bills.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose his wok job** by around 2031 and treats it as fact.
He finds safety in **public sector** slowness and union contracts.
His **pride** shows: being supported by Lena feels like letting her down.

steps.text: Save about £400 a month to reach eight months' cushion
Apply for catering jobs at the General hospital
Vote for parties promising to tax kitchen robots
Lean on Lena's (his girlfriend's) nursing pay for a while

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as the fast one, I'd say we need a plan, but I'd say it with less shouting. Five years is time for a proper debate about who pays. I'd tell people at work to start thinking now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means roughly until 2034 at the stove, so I'd be thirty-five. That's enough time for one proper move. I'd watch the ordering software take over in 2031 and know that's my three-year warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the hospital catering application in the next year or two, not rush it. I'd do a short course in diet cooking, special diets for patients, because that's a skill the robots would take longer to trust. And I'd hold off on bigger decisions until I see how the chain moves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steadier than the fast one. There's a plan forming, at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's a course in diet cooking actually like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a college certificate, about ten weeks of evenings, on allergies, soft diets, diabetic meals. A guy from my old job did it and went to a care home kitchen. It costs about four hundred pounds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hold off on bigger decisions. Which ones?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lena and I talked about buying a flat in three years. I'd want to see if the chain starts closing branches before we sign a mortgage. No point buying a flat on a wok cook's wage that might vanish.

say: I'd say five years is time for a **calmer debate** about who pays.
I'd tell colleagues to **start planning** now instead of waiting.
think: I think I cook until about **2034**, when I'd be thirty-five.
I believe the **ordering software** taking over in 2031 is my warning sign.
do: Take a **special diets** cooking course for about £400 over ten weeks.
Apply to **hospital catering** within the next two years.
Hold off on a **flat purchase** until the chain's plans are clear.
feel: He feels **anxious** but steadier, because a plan is starting to form.
S3.quote: No point buying a flat on a wok cook's wage that might vanish.
fieldNote: The five-year window lets him plan **one proper move** rather than scramble.
He picks **special diets** because he thinks robots will be trusted last there.
The **flat purchase** with Lena is the decision he'd quietly delay.

steps.text: Take a ten-week special diets cooking course at college
Apply for hospital catering within two years
Delay buying a flat with Lena until the chain's plans show

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so governments have no excuse. I'd want every cook offered a funded course. And I'd say it at work like a normal conversation, not a fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Personally, robots reach the wok around 2039 and I'd be thirty-nine or forty. My wrists probably won't last that long anyway, to be honest. So it's less about AI and more about what comes after cooking for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Lantern and go for the senior wok role first. Over a few years I'd do the special diets course and maybe a supervisor course, so I can run a hospital or care kitchen later. Lena and I would still buy the flat, maybe in three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but okay. It's a long road and I can see most of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your wrists won't last anyway. Does that change how you see the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yeah. If a robot does the heavy tossing and I do the seasoning and checking, that could actually be good for me at thirty-five. It depends who gets the money from it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a nineteen-year-old starting on the wok now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the cooking, but don't plan on doing it till you're fifty, and get a second skill by thirty. I wish someone had told me that.

say: I'd say ten years leaves **no excuse** for governments not to fund courses.
I'd talk about it at work as a **normal conversation**, not a fight.
think: I think robots reach my wok around **2039**, near age forty.
I believe my **wrists** will give out before then anyway.
do: Go for the **senior wok** role at Lantern first.
Do the special diets and **supervisor courses** over a few years.
Still **buy a flat** with Lena in about three years.
feel: He feels **uneasy but okay**, seeing most of the road ahead.
S4.quote: Learn the cooking, but don't plan on doing it till you're fifty, and get a second skill by thirty.
fieldNote: He reframes robots as possibly **helping his wrists**, depending on who benefits.
His long-term income still depends on **leaving the stove**, so he stays anxious.
His advice to young cooks is the plan he's **making for himself**.

steps.text: Apply for the senior wok role at Lantern
Take the special diets and supervisor courses over three years
Buy a flat with Lena in about three years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be out of work at thirty-one with Lena carrying us. What would help is a government plan that pays for cooks to retrain before the robots arrive, not after. And a union that's already in the room when head office decides.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about our bodies. Cooks wear out before we retire, robots or not. If a robot does the heavy lifting and the cook keeps the pay, that's progress, but if the owner keeps everything, a kitchen robot is just a sacking with extra steps.

headlineQuote: If the owner keeps everything, a kitchen robot is just a sacking with extra steps.
portrait: Ben is a **27-year-old** wok cook at a chain noodle restaurant, living with his nurse girlfriend Lena.
He's **progressive** but practical, joining the union and learning new screens to stay useful.
He feels **calm** in the flat world, mainly because of savings and Lena's steady pay.
He expects the **robot wok** to end his job, so the fast AGI picture alarms him most.
His plan is a move into **hospital catering** and special diets, where change moves slower.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028**, losing work at thirty-one while Lena carries the household.
whatWouldHelp: He wants a **government plan** that funds cooks to retrain before robots arrive.
He wants the **union** in the room when head office makes decisions.
